maling.explanation: "Maling" means "paint". To talk about a picture on a wall, use "et maleri" (a painting): "Der hænger et maleri i stuen" (A painting hangs in the living room).

man.explanation: "Man" means "you", as in anybody in general. To say something is true for anyone, use "man": "Man kan købe billetter her" (You can buy tickets here). To talk to one person, use "du" (you): "Du kan købe billetter her" (You can buy tickets here). Do not mix it up with "en mand" (a man): "Der står en mand her" (A man is standing here).

man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene.explanation: "Man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene" means "Don't judge a book by its cover". Literally, it says you should not judge the dog by its hair. The word "skue" is an old word for "look at". Use it when a person turns out different from how they looked: "Han ser sur ud." "Ja, men man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene." (He looks grumpy. Yes, but don't judge a book by its cover.)

related.en: all that glitters is not gold

mandag.explanation: "En mandag" means "a Monday". To say something happens on the coming Monday, use "på" (on): "Vi ses på mandag" (See you on Monday). To say it happens every Monday, say "om mandagen": "Jeg har fri om mandagen" (I am off on Mondays). To say last Monday, say "i mandags": "Vi mødtes i mandags" (We met last Monday). In the middle of a sentence, write the day as "mandag", not "Mandag".

mandlig.explanation: "Mandlig" means "male". It is built from "en mand" (a man). To describe a male colleague, say: "en mandlig kollega" (a male colleague). To describe an animal, use the same word: "en mandlig løve" (a male lion).

manerer.explanation: "Manerer" means "manners". To say someone is well-behaved, use "at have gode manerer" (to have good manners): "Hun har gode manerer" (She has good manners).

mange.explanation: "Mange" means "many". To talk about things you can count, put it before them: "mange biler" (many cars). To talk about something you pour or measure, use "meget" (a lot, much): "meget vand" (a lot of water).

mange tak.explanation: "Mange tak" means "Thank you very much". It is a stronger thanks than "tak" (thanks). To name what you are thankful for, add "for": "Mange tak for kaffen" (Thank you very much for the coffee). To answer, say: "Mange tak!" "Selv tak." (Thank you very much! You're welcome.)

mangelfuld.explanation: "Mangelfuld" means "inadequate". It is built from "mangel" (shortage) and "-fuld" (full of), so it is literally "full of shortage". To say information is not good enough, say: "mangelfuld information" (inadequate information).

mangfoldighed.explanation: "Mangfoldighed" means "diversity". It is built from "mangfoldig" (diverse) and the ending "-hed". The same ending makes "frihed" (freedom) from "fri" (free).

manglende.explanation: "Manglende" means "missing". It comes from the verb "at mangle" (to lack). To say that a page is missing, use the verb: "Der mangler en side" (A page is missing).

marcipan.explanation: "Marcipan" means "marzipan". A Danish Christmas treat is "en marcipangris" (a marzipan pig).

marihuana.explanation: "Marihuana" means "marijuana". Danish spells it with an "h" where English has a "j": "marihuana".

markant.explanation: "Markant" means "distinctive". To say a change is large and easy to notice, say: "en markant forbedring" (a marked improvement). To say a person stands out, say: "en markant politiker" (a prominent politician).

marmelade.explanation: "Marmelade" means "jam". Another word for jam is "syltetøj": "Jeg vil have syltetøj på brødet" (I want jam on the bread).

marmor.explanation: "Et marmor" means "marble". The word "marmor" also starts "en marmorkage" (a marble cake).

marts.explanation: "Marts" means "March". To say today's date, write the month as "marts", not "Marts": "I dag er det den tiende marts" (Today is the tenth of March).

masser af.explanation: "Masser af" means "lots of". It is literally "masses of". To say there is a large amount of something, put it before the thing: "masser af mad" (lots of food).

matematik.explanation: "Matematik" means "math". To use the short form for the school subject, say "matte": "Jeg har matte i dag" (I have math today).

materiel.explanation: "Materiel" means "material", as in things you can touch or own, not ideas or feelings: "materielle goder" (material goods). To talk about a substance such as wood, use "et materiale" (a material): "Træ er et godt materiale" (Wood is a good material).

mayonnaise.explanation: "Mayonnaise" means "mayonnaise". To shorten it, say "mayo": "Vil du have mayo på?" (Do you want mayo on it?)

med.explanation: "Med" means "with". To say you are without something, use the opposite, "uden" (without): "kaffe uden mælk" (coffee without milk). To say you will go along, put "med" after the verb: "Jeg tager med" (I will come along).

med andre ord.explanation: "Med andre ord" means "in other words". To say the same thing again or sum it up, put it before the result: "Bilen er gået i stykker. Med andre ord må vi tage toget" (The car broke down. In other words, we must take the train).

med det samme.explanation: "Med det samme" means "right away". To say something will happen soon but not now, use "om lidt" (in a little while): "Jeg kommer om lidt" (I am coming in a little while).

med forsæt.explanation: "Med forsæt" means "on purpose". It is the formal expression used in law, as in a court: "Branden blev startet med forsæt" (The fire was started on purpose). To say you did something on purpose in daily talk, use "med vilje": "Jeg gjorde det med vilje" (I did it on purpose).
